name: Moulvibazar
tagline: Tea capital of Bangladesh — rainforests with hoolock gibbons, the country's tallest waterfall, lotus lakes in the gardens, and the world's only seven-layer tea.

guide.bestTime: October to March (cool, dry — gardens, forests and waterfalls all at their best). Monsoon (June–August) for full-flow waterfalls and the Hakaluki haor at peak.
guide.gettingThere: By road from Dhaka (~190 km, ~5 hr) on the Dhaka–Sylhet highway, or by rail to Sreemangal / Kulaura / Moulvibazar on the Dhaka–Sylhet line (Parabat / Joyantika / Upaban / Kalni). Most sights cluster around Sreemangal (Lawachhara, BTRI) and Kamalganj (Madhabpur Lake, Hum Hum); Madhabkunda is in Barlekha, far to the east.
guide.difficulty: Easy to moderate — towns and tea gardens are easy; the Hum Hum trek and Patharia trails need a guide and good shoes.

mustVisit.name: Lawachhara National Park
mustVisit.description: A pocket of mixed evergreen rainforest in Sreemangal — narrow trails wind under a high canopy where hoolock gibbons call across the morning. Easy short walks for casual visitors, longer trails for the patient.
mustVisit.history: About 1,250 hectares declared a national park in 1996, carved out of the West Bhanugach reserve forest. Home to the endangered hoolock gibbon, capped langur, phayre's langur, pythons, and a long bird list; the Khasia Punji of Magurchhara sits inside the forest. Bisected by the Dhaka–Sylhet railway line.

practical.hours: Sunrise to sunset; arrive at dawn for gibbons and birds
practical.entryFee: Forest Department entry fee + guide fee

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: About 8 km east of Sreemangal town, off the Sreemangal–Bhanugach road
howToReach.transport: CNG / reserved car from Sreemangal town

mustVisit.bestTime: October to March; arrive at dawn for wildlife
tips: Hire a Forest Department guide at the gate — trails fork and the gibbons need spotting
Wear closed shoes and long sleeves — leeches appear after rain
Keep your voice down on the trail; gibbons move off at noise

mustVisit.name: Madhabkunda Waterfall
mustVisit.description: Bangladesh's tallest waterfall — water drops some 60 metres off the Patharia hills into a wide rocky pool. The walk in is short, the spray is constant, and on a clear afternoon you can wade to the foot of the fall.
mustVisit.history: Set in the Patharia hill range of Barlekha, the falls and surrounding forest were turned into an eco-park by the Forest Department. A Khasi village sits nearby and a smaller fall, Parikunda, lies a short trek into the woods behind.

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: About 70 km east of Moulvibazar town, in Barlekha Upazila; or by train to Kulaura then road
howToReach.transport: Bus / CNG to Madhabkunda gate from Moulvibazar or Kulaura

mustVisit.bestTime: June to October — fall is in full flow; the rocks are slippery so wear sandals with grip
tips: Trek the extra 30 minutes to Parikunda — quieter and quite beautiful
Pakhipath bridge near the entrance is a good photograph spot
Avoid swimming directly under the fall — rocks tumble after rain

mustVisit.name: Madhabpur Lake
mustVisit.description: A long, narrow lake carved out of three small hills inside the Patrakhola tea estate — its surface stippled with red, white and blue lotus and lily. The classic Sreemangal photograph: tea-bushes climbing one bank, lotus opening on the water.
mustVisit.history: Built in 1965 by Patrakhola Tea Estate to store irrigation water for the gardens, the 50-acre lake quickly became famous for its lotus blooms. It lies in Madhabpur Union of Kamalganj Upazila, about 12 km east of Sreemangal.

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: About 50 km west of Moulvibazar town, in Kamalganj Upazila; ~12 km east of Sreemangal
howToReach.transport: CNG / car from Sreemangal town through Bhanugach into the tea estate

mustVisit.bestTime: September to December — lotus at peak; mornings are quietest
tips: Ask permission at the tea-estate office before walking the inner paths
Pair with Lawachhara on the same day — they're 20 minutes apart
The blue water-lily is rare; look along the far edges

mustVisit.name: Hum Hum Waterfall
mustVisit.description: A hidden fall deep in the Rajkandi reserve forest — reached by a 2-3 hour trek through streams, bamboo and hill-paths. About 50 metres tall, found only in 2010, and still the wildest cascade in the country.
mustVisit.history: Lies in Kurma reserve forest of Kamalganj, on the edge of the Tripura border. The fall went unmapped for decades because the trail crosses streams in and out — local Tipra and Manipuri trackers were the first to lead outsiders in.

practical.entryFee: Forest entry + mandatory local guide fee

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: About 55 km from Moulvibazar via Kamalganj; reserved car to Kolabon Para, then trek
howToReach.transport: CNG / car to Kolabon Para village, then 2-3 hr trek with a local guide

mustVisit.bestTime: July to October — full flow; avoid going right after heavy rain (flash currents)
tips: Hire a local Tipra guide at Kolabon — the trail crosses streams and is easy to lose
Wear closed-toe waterproof sandals; carry water and a light bag only
Plan for a full day; leeches are common after rain

mustVisit.name: Sreemangal Tea Country & BTRI
mustVisit.description: The town that calls itself Bangladesh's tea capital — endless rolling estates, the Bangladesh Tea Research Institute, the world-famous seven-layer tea, and roads where workers, baskets full, walk back from the bushes at dusk.
mustVisit.history: Tea came here in the late 19th century after the success of Sylhet's Malnicherra; today Sreemangal and Kamalganj together hold the densest cluster of tea estates in the country. BTRI was set up in 1957 as a Pakistan Tea Board station and re-formed as the national institute in 1973.

practical.hours: Estates are private; the BTRI campus is visitable by request

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: Sreemangal town is about 40 km southwest of Moulvibazar town on the Sylhet line
howToReach.transport: Train to Sreemangal, then CNG / rickshaw around the gardens

mustVisit.bestTime: October to March — clear, cool air, full bushes
tips: Walk garden paths in early morning or late afternoon light
Drink the seven-layer tea where it was invented (Sreemangal town)
Always ask permission of garden staff before stepping into the rows

mustVisit.name: Hakaluki Haor
mustVisit.description: One of Bangladesh's largest haors — a vast freshwater wetland that swells to over 18,000 hectares in the monsoon and dries to a chain of beels in winter, drawing tens of thousands of migratory waterbirds.
mustVisit.history: Spread across Barlekha, Juri, Kulaura, Fenchuganj and Golapganj, declared an Ecologically Critical Area and recognised as a Ramsar wetland of international importance for its bird, fish and freshwater diversity.

practical.hours: Daylight hours; access by country boat

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: About 60–80 km northeast of Moulvibazar; the main boat ghats sit in Barlekha and Juri
howToReach.transport: Bus / reserved car to Barlekha or Juri, then engine boat across the haor

mustVisit.bestTime: Monsoon (Jun–Sep) for the full haor; Nov–Feb for migratory birds at the beels
tips: Carry binoculars — the bird list is the real attraction
Use local boatmen — they know which beels still hold water in the dry season
Sunset on the water is the photograph; head out by 4 pm in winter

specialties.name: Seven-Layer Tea (Sat Rong Cha)
specialties.description: Invented by Romesh Ram Gour at his Nilkantha Cha Cabin in Sreemangal in 2002 — seven layers of differently spiced tea, each a different colour and density, poured to settle one above the other.

specialties.name: Sreemangal Estate Tea
specialties.description: Strong, fresh tea poured straight from the country's densest cluster of tea gardens. A glass at a tea-garden canteen in Bhanugach or Finlay Tea is the simplest local pleasure.

specialties.name: Manipuri Bamboo-Shoot Curry
specialties.description: From the Manipuri community of Kamalganj — fresh bamboo shoots cooked into a sour, fragrant curry. Best alongside hidol (fermented fish) chutney and rice.

bucketlist.title: Hear hoolock gibbons in Lawachhara at dawn
bucketlist.detail: Be at the gate before sunrise — the gibbons call across the canopy in the first hour of light, the most arresting sound in a Bangladeshi forest.

bucketlist.title: Stand under Madhabkunda's spray
bucketlist.detail: Bangladesh's tallest waterfall — 60 metres of water onto a rock pool. Walk through the spray, then trek 30 minutes to Parikunda fall behind it.

bucketlist.title: Catch the lotus in bloom at Madhabpur Lake
bucketlist.detail: A long lake carved out of three hills inside Patrakhola Tea Estate, its surface stippled with red, white and rare blue water-lily — Sreemangal's signature postcard.

bucketlist.title: Trek to Hum Hum waterfall
bucketlist.detail: A two-to-three-hour walk through bamboo, streams and hill-paths into the Rajkandi reserve to a 50-metre cascade unmapped until 2010 — the wildest day-hike in Bangladesh.

bucketlist.title: Drink seven-layer tea where it was invented
bucketlist.detail: Romesh Ram Gour layered seven different teas in 2002 at his small cabin in Ramnagar — Sreemangal's most photographed glass. Imitators are everywhere; the original is here.

bucketlist.title: Walk the rows at BTRI
bucketlist.detail: Bangladesh Tea Research Institute's 1957 campus is the lab and lecture hall of the country's tea — clones, trials, drying sheds and lots of fresh estate tea.

bucketlist.title: Visit a Manipuri Palli in Kamalganj
bucketlist.detail: Bamboo-shoot curries, hand-woven shawls and the Rashlila dance — the Manipuri community of Kamalganj have kept their language and ritual alive for two centuries since arriving from the Imphal valley.

bucketlist.title: Sit in a Khasia Punji and chew paan
bucketlist.detail: Khasi villages inside Lawachhara grow paan vines on trees and welcome visitors warmly — bring a small gift, sit on a cane mat, drink red tea.

bucketlist.title: Watch migratory birds at Hakaluki Haor
bucketlist.detail: Bangladesh's biggest haor, a Ramsar wetland — tens of thousands of waterbirds in winter and the kind of horizon-wide sunset that justifies binoculars.

bucketlist.title: Catch the Manipuri Rashlila on Kartik Purnima
bucketlist.detail: The single great festival of the Bishnupriya Manipuri community — overnight dance honouring Krishna and Radha, performed at Madhabpur and Adampur for over a century.

bucketlist.title: Pay respects at the Hamidur Rahman memorial
bucketlist.detail: Bir Sreshtho sepoy Mohammad Hamidur Rahman was killed on 28 October 1971 silencing a Pakistan Army machine-gun at Dhalai, Kamalganj — the only Liberation War battlefield in the country marked for a Bir Sreshtho.

bucketlist.title: Ride the Dhaka–Sylhet train through the tea hills
bucketlist.detail: The line slices straight through Lawachhara and the tea estates — between Bhairab and Sreemangal the windows are an unbroken green corridor of bushes and rainforest.

foods.name: Seven-Layer Tea (Sat Rong Cha)
foods.description: Invented in Sreemangal by Romesh Ram Gour in 2002 — seven layers of differently spiced tea poured to settle one above the other. The most photographed glass in Bangladesh.

foods.name: Sreemangal Estate Tea
foods.description: Fresh, strong tea from the country's densest cluster of estates — drink it where the bushes climb the hill behind you.

foods.name: Manipuri Bamboo-Shoot Curry
foods.description: A sour, fragrant curry made with fresh bamboo shoots — the signature dish of the Bishnupriya Manipuri community of Kamalganj.

foods.name: Shatkora Beef
foods.description: The greater-Sylhet hallmark — beef cooked with shatkora citrus for a fragrant, bittersweet gravy.

famousPeople.name: Dwijen Sharma
famousPeople.knownFor: Naturalist, botanist and one of the foundational figures of Bangla science writing — author of over thirty books on trees, gardens and the natural world. Born in Shimulia village of Barlekha Upazila in Moulvibazar; awarded the Bangla Academy Literary Award (1987) and Ekushey Padak (2015).

famousPeople.name: Bir Sreshtho Mohammad Hamidur Rahman
famousPeople.knownFor: Sepoy of the Bangladesh Forces who silenced a Pakistan Army machine-gun in hand-to-hand combat at Dhalai, Kamalganj, on 28 October 1971 and was killed in the action. Posthumously awarded the Bir Sreshtho, Bangladesh's highest gallantry honour. Born in Jhenaidah; the Moulvibazar battlefield and memorial are where his story ends.

didYouKnow: Madhabkunda Waterfall in Barlekha is Bangladesh's tallest, dropping about 60 metres off the Patharia hills.
Lawachhara National Park's 1,250 hectares are home to the endangered hoolock gibbon — one of the few places left in Bangladesh where you can hear them call at dawn.
Sreemangal's seven-layer tea was invented in 2002 by Romesh Ram Gour at his Nilkantha Cha Cabin — celebrities, ambassadors and visitors from more than a hundred countries have since come to drink it.
Madhabpur Lake in Kamalganj was dug in 1965 by Patrakhola Tea Estate to store irrigation water; it is now famous for its lotus blooms and giant water-lily.
Hakaluki Haor is one of Bangladesh's largest haors and a Ramsar wetland of international importance — a critical wintering ground for migratory waterbirds.
Bangladesh Tea Research Institute (BTRI) was founded in Sreemangal in 1957 as the Pakistan Tea Research Station and re-formed under its current name in 1973.
Bir Sreshtho Mohammad Hamidur Rahman, one of only seven recipients of Bangladesh's highest gallantry honour, was killed at Dhalai in Kamalganj on 28 October 1971.
